#+title: Native libraries as prepared artifacts

Read [[file:artifact-workflows.org][daily workflows and the capability roster]] for editing, debugging and
multi-session use. The executable example is in =examples/artifacts=.

* Build a library once and use its exact bytes
A native product contains a shared library and a manifest naming its source
snapshot, target, compiler identity, ABI requirement and SHA256. Nix builds the
product from the platform's pinned flake.lock. Beam Lisp checks the manifest
and library before selecting it. A selection is a symlink to immutable store
bytes; a failed preparation leaves the selected library in place.

Cargo still resolves and builds the Rust crate inside the Nix derivation.
Nix supplies its pinned toolchain, vendored dependencies and private build
directory, then publishes the immutable product for Beam Lisp to verify.

The managed backend supports standalone, locked Rust cdylib crates on
x86_64-linux. Registry dependencies are vendored by Nix. Crate snapshots include
build.rs, Cargo configuration and supporting files; target/, .git/ and .bl/
are reserved generated directories. Source symlinks are refused. Workspace/path
dependencies outside the crate need a separate declared source-closure recipe.

* Start the checkout
Run the ordinary checkout command:

#+begin_src sh
./bin/bl eval '(println 42)'
#+end_src

Before starting BEAM, the launcher prepares a retained Nix platform containing
its native transport, pinned OTP/Elixir, trusted recipes and the engine's native
products. The checkout includes its GTK/WebKit product; server drop production
selects the six server products. Cargo runs inside bounded Nix workers. It is
not required on the caller's PATH.

The platform cache under .bl/platforms is keyed by complete native/tool inputs,
including executable modes and new files not yet staged in Git. Rust edits
prepare a new product; application-only edits reuse the platform. Every native
selection is established before SDK native-host identities are frozen. Use
--cold for an explicitly fresh VM and realm stop to stop a checkout's warm VM.

* Prepare from the checkout
Use a trusted platform checkout containing flake.lock and nix/native-artifact.nix.
The Nix client and systemd user manager must be available. The platform is trusted
build code; project requests contain data.

#+begin_src sh
./bin/bl artifacts prepare "$PWD/native/lazy_memo" lazy_memo beam-lisp-native-lazy_memo-v1
./bin/bl artifacts list
#+end_src

Each preparation prints a JSON receipt and registers its own Nix retention root.
Receipts live under $XDG_CACHE_HOME/beam_lisp/artifacts, or
~/.cache/beam_lisp/artifacts. Their native-*/receipt.json files can be inspected
with ordinary tools. Roots remain until deliberately removed by their owner;
automatic pruning requires a complete live-consumer retention policy.

The first request may fetch dependencies and compile Rust. An unchanged request
reuses the product. Updating an application's .bl files leaves a standalone
native crate's snapshot unchanged. Updating Rust, a build script, Cargo config,
a lockfile or the pinned toolchain participates in its build identity.

* Declare a project native
Nix is the production backend. Projects keep their ordinary declarations:

#+begin_src clojure
{:name "search-service"
 :paths ["src"]
 :build {:native ["native/*"]}}
#+end_src

Keep Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and the supporting source inputs in each declared
crate. Use the normal build command. build/build-native-crate,
build/build-native and runtime native refresh consume the same immutable
product contract. There is no mutable Cargo producer fallback. The managed
launcher supplies BL_ARTIFACT_PLATFORM; advanced API callers pass a trusted
platform explicitly. BL_NATIVE_PROVIDER=local is unsupported.

A successful native build selects priv/native/<crate>.so under destination
custody. Nix-backed selections refer directly to a store library. Already loaded
native code stays bound to its loaded library; native changes require a fresh
VM. The runtime's actual NIF module, function and arity checks govern loading.
An ABI label in a receipt expresses a consumer requirement, not a proof of ABI
compatibility or an execution grant.

* Compare candidates
Use receipt paths printed by preparation or found with artifacts list.

#+begin_src sh
./bin/bl artifacts compare /path/to/first/receipt.json /path/to/second/receipt.json
#+end_src

The report names changed source, target, ABI requirement, toolchain and library
identity. It reports identity differences; runtime compatibility and migration
have their own checks. Compilation and metadata assembly are separate Nix
products, so a changed consumer ABI label reuses identical compiled Rust bytes.

* Keep a reproducible bug descriptor
#+begin_src sh
./bin/bl artifacts capsule /path/to/receipt.json "$PWD/capsules"
#+end_src

A new capsule directory retains the verified product and records the immutable
source request, manifest, compiler key and the loaded native runtime identity.
Its qualification field is not-recorded: attaching test evidence is a separate
operation. Mutable databases, application secrets and shell environments are
outside this descriptor. Copying it to another machine also requires making its
store objects available there, for example through an authorized Nix store copy
or configured substituter.

* Call a prepared NIF
The executable showcase lives in examples/artifacts. It prepares artifact_demo,
selects the store library, loads its real Rustler host and checks answer() = 42.

#+begin_src sh
./bin/bl --cold run examples/artifacts/showcase.bl
#+end_src

Read native/artifact_demo/src/lib.rs and src/artifact/showcase.bl inside that
example together: the Rustler module name matches the Beam Lisp host name.
Use a fresh VM after changing the native source. Multiple preparations and
comparison can run independently of activation.

* Use the library API
#+begin_src clojure
(ns my.preparation (:require [artifact :as artifact]))

(def product
  (artifact/prepare-native!
    {:platform "/trusted/beam-lisp"
     :source "/project/native/search"
     :crate "search"
     :abi "search-api-v1"
     :target "x86_64-linux"
     :timeout-ms 300000
     :memory-bytes 1073741824}))

(:library product)       ; immutable library path
(:request product)       ; immutable source snapshot and requested contract
(:retention-root product)
(artifact/verify! (:output product) (:request product))
#+end_src

The process adapter preserves Nix's JSON stdout separately from progress logs.
External client jobs have deadlines, memory/swap limits and cgroup cleanup.
Nix daemon workers have their own resource boundary: client limits do not cap
those workers. Rust workers run in KVM guests with fixed RAM, zero swap and
finite disk-backed scratch space. Server native workers have 3072 MiB; the
GTK/WebKit worker has 6144 MiB. The NixOS host module also configures aggregate
daemon limits. Configured Nix builders supply remote execution; their logs
identify the worker actually used.

Nix artifacts retain their source and compiled product. Toolchain metadata uses
a fingerprint rather than a compiler-output reference, keeping native runtime
closures smaller. Reproduction may still require fetching the pinned compiler
and dependency inputs. A shipped FHS drop can carry the selected library without
requiring a Nix installation on its destination host.

* Pin the provider in a managed environment
The flake exports artifact-platform: a small store object containing the trusted
recipes and lockfile. It is independent of the compiler and application payload.

#+begin_src sh
nix build .#artifact-platform
export BL_ARTIFACT_PLATFORM="$(readlink -f result)"
#+end_src

Managed NixOS build hosts can import the artifacts module from this flake:

#+begin_src nix
{
  imports = [ beam-lisp.nixosModules.artifacts ];
  services.beam-lisp-artifacts = {
    enable = true;
    maxJobs = 1;
    daemonMemoryMax = "8G";
    daemonMemorySwapMax = "1G";
  };
}
#+end_src

The module sets a strict sandbox, disables sandbox fallback, enables Nix build
cgroups, bounds the daemon's aggregate memory/swap and publishes the immutable
platform path to sessions. Its policy applies to the host's shared Nix daemon,
so choose limits for the whole build host. Apply it through the normal host
configuration deployment and validate actual worker containment afterward.
Unprivileged clients cannot enforce restricted daemon settings themselves.
Each remote builder needs its own accepted worker policy.

* Cold commands use a staged executor
The immutable platform carries bin/bl-command-executor and executor.json.
Filesystem-writing Source commands verify its digest and protocol before handing
their real kernel loans to the service manager. A trusted checkout platform can
stage this product through nix/prepare-platform.nix; ambient Cargo is unnecessary.
Drops can use their own compatible launcher, and checkout transport builds use
BL_ROOT to locate the staged launcher independently of the project's directory.

Keep secrets outside crate source directories: source snapshots enter the shared
Nix store. Capsules retain an artifact and its derivation identity; reconstructing
its build also requires the referenced store inputs and pinned recipes.
